subtype: Approach: keeps batches but adds a quick way to reach her for urgent items [Revision]
passage:
In the Lisbon office, Marta had kept two mail slots a day, at eleven and at four, for three weeks, and her code was better for it. Then Rafael, who worked on the payment team, caught her in the corridor. "Last Thursday a server alarm was in my message to you at nine and you saw it at eleven," he said. "Nothing burned, but I was sweating."

Marta thought about it. She did not want to go back to a beeping inbox. That evening she wrote to the team: "I still read email at eleven and four. For anything urgent, call or text this number. If it isn't urgent, it waits." She put the number on the shared page and silenced her alerts again. The next week Rafael called once, at noon, about an outage, and Marta answered on the second ring. The rest of her mornings stayed quiet.

qa.q: At what times does Marta read email?
qa.a: Marta reads email at eleven and at four.

qa.q: How did Marta feel about going back to a beeping inbox?
qa.a: Marta was reluctant to go back to a beeping inbox, because her quiet mail slots had made her code better.

qa.q: What could Marta and Rafael agree so that the urgent number is used well?
qa.a: They could agree what counts as urgent, such as outages, so that calls are kept for real emergencies.

qa.q: How might Rafael have seen Marta's new number?
qa.a: Rafael might feel relieved to have a reliable route for real emergencies, since his worry was answered.

grounding: Shows a person keeping two mail slots and sharing a number for urgent items so focus stays without blocking emergencies.

subtype: Approach: makes a public promise to keep on track [Action]
passage: Anjali, come, I will tell you about the time Dorje bragged. I was fifteen, and I had started a coding tutorial three times and quit three times. One Sunday, half joking, I typed into our class group: "I will finish the whole coding tutorial in thirty days." Thumbs-ups came back, and one boy wrote, "Let's see." My ears went hot. I did not want to look foolish. So I took a pencil and drew a chart on the door: one hour every evening after dinner, seven to eight. On the lazy days, the chart and the group were both staring at me. I finished on day twenty-nine. I still think about how the promise pushed me on the tired days.

qa.q: How many days did Dorje promise?
qa.a: Dorje promised thirty days.

qa.q: How did Dorje feel when the boy wrote "Let's see"?
qa.a: Dorje felt embarrassed and did not want to look foolish.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story helped Dorje keep the promise?
qa.a: Drawing a chart for one hour every evening, seven to eight, turned the promise into a daily routine.

qa.q: How might the classmate who wrote "Let's see" have viewed the promise?
qa.a: The classmate might have doubted it, since it was a big claim, and may have felt impressed when it was finished.

grounding: Shows a teenager promising the class group to finish a coding tutorial and setting a daily hour so as not to look foolish.

passage:
Three days before the first paper, Nihal opened his phone and looked at the racing game he played every night. He pressed and held the icon, and deleted it. Then, before lights out, he unplugged his charger and walked to Parth's bed.

"Keep this till seven."

"Seriously?" said Parth. "Your phone is at eleven percent. It'll die by midnight."

"That's the plan."

The first night Nihal lay awake wanting to check something, anything. The second night he read organic chemistry until sleep came. On the morning of the paper he collected his charger, and his phone showed forty-four unread messages that could wait.

qa.a: Nihal felt restless and tempted, lying awake wanting to check something.

qa.q: What could Nihal do if the phone is needed in an emergency at night?
qa.a: Nihal could agree with Parth that the charger comes back for a real need, so that the rule bends without breaking.

qa.q: How might Parth feel about keeping the charger?
qa.a: Parth might feel a bit amused and doubtful, judging from "Seriously?", but still willing to help.

grounding: Shows a student before exams deleting a game and handing the charger to a roommate at night so distraction is harder than study.

subtype: Approach: pays or books something in advance to create a cost for quitting [Thinking]
passage: Aparna here. Harsha, who sits opposite me at the design studio, told me over lunch what he had done. "I paid for three months at the gym, all at once," he said. "I know myself. If I pay month to month, I'll skip and tell myself I'll pay next time. But money already gone will make me feel silly for not going." He said it like a rule he had checked. The first week I saw his gym bag under the desk every morning. On day nine it stayed on the chair and he left at six sharp. I don't know if he enjoys it or just doesn't want to waste the money. When I asked, he shrugged and said, "Either is fine with me."

qa.q: How many months did Harsha pay for?
qa.a: Harsha paid for three months, all at once.

qa.q: What did Harsha expect from paying everything at once?
qa.a: Harsha expected that money already gone would make him feel silly for skipping, so he would go.

qa.q: What could Harsha do if he still skips despite having paid?
qa.a: Harsha could add a workout partner or fixed times in his calendar, since the payment alone may not be enough.

qa.q: Why can Aparna not say whether Harsha enjoys the gym?

grounding: Shows a worker paying for a three-month plan upfront, expecting money already spent to make him attend.

subtype: Approach: sets a device so strict that it backfires [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday, 9:30 pm. Well, that plan is dead. On Monday I set a blocker to lock every app on my phone, all day, no exceptions. No messages, no maps, no bank. I thought: cold turkey, total focus. Today at eleven, Ishita sent a photo of the client's signed form on the work chat and asked me to forward it within ten minutes. My phone would not open the chat. I hunted for a way round it, panicked, deleted the blocker altogether, and still sent the form twenty minutes late. Now everything is open again and I scrolled for an hour tonight. The rule was too strict. It never made room for the one app I actually need.

Naveen

qa.q: What did Ishita ask Naveen to do?
qa.a: Ishita asked Naveen to forward the client's signed form within ten minutes.

qa.q: How does Naveen feel about the plan now?
qa.a: Naveen feels frustrated and a little defeated, calling the plan dead.

qa.q: What could Naveen do differently next time?
qa.a: Naveen could set a lighter lock that blocks only the distracting apps and keeps the work chat open.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt while waiting for the form?
qa.a: Ishita may have felt anxious about the deadline and puzzled about why Naveen was unreachable.

grounding: Shows Naveen locking all apps for a day, breaking the lock in a hurry when work needs one and dropping the system.

subtype: Approach: loosens the rule and keeps the parts that helped [Revision]
passage: Yogesh, you look like Nikhil did at your age: phone in hand, guilt on the face. Let me tell you what I did. I once locked all my apps from nine to six, because games were eating my life. For three days I felt strong. On the fourth day my manager needed a file and my work chat was locked. I broke the lock in a panic and dropped the whole thing for a month. Then I sat down and asked: what was working? The evening games block was working. What was not? Blocking the work apps. So I made the rule smaller: games locked from six to eleven at night, work apps free at all times. It still holds two years later.

qa.q: When are games locked under the new rule?
qa.a: Games are locked from six to eleven at night.

qa.q: How did Nikhil feel on the fourth day when the manager needed the file?
qa.a: Nikhil felt panicked, and broke the lock in a hurry.

qa.q: Which turning point inside the story helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking what was working and what was not showed that the games block helped while blocking work apps hurt, so only the second part was changed.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt while waiting for the file?
qa.a: The manager might have felt impatient or worried about the delay, and puzzled that Nikhil could not open the chat.

grounding: Shows a person loosening a strict phone lock, keeping the evening games block and freeing work apps during the day.

subtype: Approach: studies with a friend who has a similar goal [Thinking]
passage: In the school hostel study hall, Akash sat with his phone, thinking about a lazy evening. Then he remembered: seven o'clock, call with Usha. Yesterday they had agreed that both would be on a call, cameras off, each would say a target, and then they would work for forty minutes. "If I'm late, Usha waits, and I'll feel bad," he whispered to himself. He opened the physics book at five to seven. At seven Usha's voice came: "Ready? I'm doing two history chapters." "Numericals from chapter six," said Akash. They went quiet. When the call ended, he had done nine problems, on an evening he would normally have spent on videos. "Same time tomorrow," said Usha.

qa.q: What did Akash plan to work on during the call?
qa.a: Akash planned numericals from chapter six.

qa.q: How was Akash feeling as he considered a lazy evening?
qa.a: Akash was tempted by a lazy evening, but felt it would be unfair to keep Usha waiting, and that guilt pushed him to start.

qa.q: What could Akash and Usha add to keep the habit going?
qa.a: They could share one line about what they finished at the end of each call, or agree what to do if one cannot join.

qa.q: How might Usha feel about Akash arriving on time?
qa.a: Usha may feel supported and encouraged, since each of them starting on time helps both.

grounding: Shows a teenager pairing with a classmate for evening study calls and starting on time because someone is waiting.

subtype: Approach: agrees to report progress to a friend [Action]

Night 12. Texted Salma: "Six hours. Done." Salma sent back: "Five and a half, chemistry mock. Streak 12 nights!" We started this after the coaching test results, when we both slid into evenings of scrolling. The rule is small: before sleep, text the hours studied, even if the number is low. Some nights it is two hours and a joke. Tonight was good; I finished the whole polity list. I noticed that I look forward to that little message, and I do not want to type "zero" after eleven nights of numbers. Tomorrow's paper is at nine, so no more scrolling. Salma says whoever breaks the streak buys the tea.

Siddharth

subtype: Approach: picks a partner who excuses everything [Pitfall]
passage: With two weeks before the final exam, Aditi asked her close friend Siddharth to be her check-in partner. "Every night, ask whether I did my hours," she said. Night one, she had done two hours of four. "It's fine," said Siddharth. "You've been working hard. Take a break." Night two, one hour. "Honestly, me too. Let's watch one episode." By night six the check-ins were texts like "ugh, same" and "tomorrow?" Nobody pushed. The pile of unfinished chapters stayed exactly the same size. On night twelve Aditi looked at the calendar and saw two days left. She felt sick. She had told herself that the partner was helping, and all they had really shared was excuses.

qa.q: How many hours of the four had Aditi done on the first night?
qa.a: Aditi had done two hours of four on night one.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel on night twelve?
qa.a: Aditi felt sick with worry and regret at how little had changed.

qa.q: What could Aditi look for in a partner instead?
qa.a: Aditi could look for a partner who asks honestly about the plan and gently says when a target was missed, or add a written goal.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have meant "Take a break"?
qa.a: Siddharth probably meant it kindly, wanting Aditi to rest, without seeing that it hurt her plan.

grounding: Shows a student choosing a partner who excuses everything so the check-ins become shared excuses and nothing changes.

subtype: Approach: asks a colleague to check milestones weekly [Action]
passage: I'm Pranati, and for two years the certification exam lived in a folder called someday. Last September I made a plan: twelve weeks, one module a week. Then I asked Kamal, a colleague in the finance team, if we could meet every Friday at four for ten minutes. I would show what I had finished, and Kamal would only ask, "Is that what you planned?" No advice, no praise. The first Friday I had not finished the module and my face went hot. The second Friday I had. By week eight I noticed I was starting on Monday mornings just so my page would not look empty on Friday. I passed on the first try. I still keep Fridays with Kamal for other things.

qa.q: When did Pranati and Kamal meet?
qa.a: They met every Friday at four for ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Pranati feel on the first Friday?
qa.a: Pranati felt embarrassed, with a hot face, since the module was not finished.

qa.q: What could Pranati do if a Friday module is missed?
qa.a: Pranati could tell Kamal honestly and add a catch-up slot to the plan rather than hiding it.

qa.q: How might Kamal see the Friday meetings?
qa.a: Kamal might feel useful and glad that one simple question was enough to help.

grounding: Shows a young professional showing a colleague each Friday what was done on a certification plan and keeping to the schedule.
